CALIFORNIA ONLINE PRIVACY PROTECTION ACT (CALOPPA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · https://www.acme.com

DUTY TO CONSPICUOUSLY POST A PRIVACY POLICY, AND THE 30-DAY CURE PERIOD
California law requires an operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information through the Internet about individual consumers residing in California who use or visit that Web site or online service to conspicuously post its privacy policy on the Web site, or, in the case of an operator of an online service, to make that policy available by one of the alternative means the statute recognizes for online services. An operator is in violation of this posting duty only if it fails to post its policy within 30 days after being notified of noncompliance — the statute builds in a cure period rather than imposing liability for a first, uncured lapse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) An operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information through the Internet about individual consumers residing in California who use or visit its commercial Web site or online service shall conspicuously post its privacy policy on its Web site, or in the case of an operator of an online service, make that policy available in accordance with paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 22577. An operator shall be in violation of this subdivision only if the operator fails to post its policy within 30 days after being notified of noncompliance."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22575(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Online Privacy Protection Act, duty to conspicuously post a privacy policy and 30-day cure period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22575.)

That subdivision's own text cross-references "paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 22577" for the alternative means by which an operator of an online service (as opposed to a Web site) may make its policy available; this document verifies and quotes that cross-referenced provision independently in a separate clause below (§ 22577(b)), so the two clauses together, though drawn from different sections of the same chapter, cover the full posting-method rule. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA website-privacy-policy-posting requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator; CalOPPA is narrower than, and predates, the California Consumer Privacy Act, and this document does not address CCPA's substantive consumer rights, which are covered in this site's separate CCPA consumer-facing disclosure document. This clause does not determine whether a specific website or service is "commercial," whether a specific visitor "resides in California," or whether a specific operator has in fact been "notified of noncompliance" so as to start the 30-day cure period running — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF THE PRIVACY POLICY: CATEGORIES OF PII AND THIRD PARTIES, REVIEW PROCESS, CHANGE NOTIFICATION, AND EFFECTIVE DATE
California law requires that the privacy policy an operator posts under CalOPPA identify the categories of personally identifiable information the operator collects through its Web site or online service about individual consumers who use or visit it, and the categories of third-party persons or entities with whom the operator may share that personally identifiable information. If — but only if — the operator maintains a process for an individual consumer to review and request changes to his or her personally identifiable information collected through the Web site or online service, the policy must describe that process; the statute does not itself require an operator to establish such a review-and-change process, only to describe one if it has one. The policy must also describe the process by which the operator notifies consumers of material changes to its privacy policy, and must identify the policy's effective date.

(2) If the operator maintains a process for an individual consumer who uses or visits its commercial Web site or online service to review and request changes to any of his or her personally identifiable information that is collected through the Web site or online service, provide a description of that process. (3) Describe the process by which the operator notifies consumers who use or visit its commercial Web site or online service of material changes to the operator’s privacy policy for that Web site or online service. (4) Identify its effective date."
  — Cal. DISCLOSURE OF "DO NOT TRACK" RESPONSE AND CROSS-SITE TRACKING BY OTHER PARTIES
California law requires that the privacy policy also disclose how the operator responds to Web browser "do not track" signals or other mechanisms that give consumers the ability to exercise choice regarding the collection of personally identifiable information about an individual consumer's online activities over time and across third-party Web sites or online services — but only if the operator engages in that kind of collection. Separately, the policy must disclose whether other parties may collect personally identifiable information about a consumer's online activities over time and across different Web sites when the consumer uses the operator's Web site or service. The statute allows an operator to satisfy the "do not track" response disclosure by providing a clear and conspicuous hyperlink in its privacy policy to an online location containing a description, including the effects, of any program or protocol the operator follows that offers the consumer that choice.

(6) Disclose whether other parties may collect personally identifiable information about an individual consumer’s online activities over time and across different Web sites when a consumer uses the operator’s Web site or service. (7) An operator may satisfy the requirement of paragraph (5) by providing a clear and conspicuous hyperlink in the operator’s privacy policy to an online location containing a description, including the effects, of any program or protocol the operator follows that offers the consumer that choice."
  — Cal. STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "PERSONALLY IDENTIFIABLE INFORMATION" AND "OPERATOR"
California law defines "personally identifiable information," for purposes of this chapter, as individually identifiable information about an individual consumer that is collected online by the operator from that individual and maintained by the operator in an accessible form, including a first and last name; a home or other physical address, including street name and city or town; an email address; a telephone number; a Social Security number; any other identifier that permits the physical or online contacting of a specific individual; and information concerning a user that the Web site or online service collects online from the user and maintains in personally identifiable form in combination with any of the identifiers just listed. Separately, California law defines "operator," for purposes of this chapter, as any person or entity that owns a Web site located on the Internet or an online service that collects and maintains personally identifiable information from a California-resident consumer who uses or visits it, where the Web site or online service is operated for commercial purposes; the definition expressly excludes a third party that operates, hosts, or manages — but does not own — a Web site or online service on the owner's behalf, or that processes information on the owner's behalf.

(6) Any other identifier that permits the physical or online contacting of a specific individual. WHAT COUNTS AS "CONSPICUOUSLY POST" UNDER THE STATUTE
California law defines "conspicuously post," with respect to a privacy policy, to include posting it by any of several methods: a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if that page is the homepage or the first significant page after entering the Web site; an icon that hyperlinks to a Web page where the actual policy is posted, if the icon is on the homepage or first significant page, contains the word "privacy," and uses a color that contrasts with the page's background or is otherwise distinguishable; a text link that hyperlinks to a Web page where the actual policy is posted, if the link is on the homepage or first significant page and either includes the word "privacy," is written in capital letters at least as large as the surrounding text, or is written in larger, contrasting, or otherwise set-off type that calls attention to it; any other functional hyperlink displayed so that a reasonable person would notice it; or, in the case of an online service, any other reasonably accessible means of making the privacy policy available to the online service's consumers.

VIOLATION STANDARD, CHAPTER OPERATIVE DATE, AND PREEMPTION OF LOCAL PRIVACY-POSTING LAWS
California law provides that an operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information from individual California-resident consumers who use or visit it is in violation of this chapter if it fails to comply with the posting requirement described elsewhere in this Notice, or with the provisions of its own posted privacy policy, and does so either knowingly and willfully, or negligently and materially — a mental-state and materiality threshold, rather than strict liability for any noncompliance. This chapter became operative on July 1, 2004. Separately, the Legislature declared that this chapter addresses a matter of statewide concern, and that it supersedes and preempts all rules, regulations, codes, ordinances, and other laws adopted by a city, county, city and county, municipality, or local agency regarding the posting of a privacy policy on an Internet Web site.

PRIVACY POLICY POSTING DECLARATION AND REQUIRED CONTENT
Acme, Inc. operates the commercial Web site or online service located at https://www.acme.com, which collects personally identifiable information through the Internet about individual consumers residing in California who use or visit it. Acme, Inc. conspicuously posts a privacy policy on that Web site or online service disclosing the following: the categories of personally identifiable information Acme, Inc. collects, and the categories of third-party persons or entities with whom Acme, Inc. may share that information: Identifiers (name, email address), internet activity (browsing history on our site), and geolocation data; the categories of third parties described further as: Analytics providers, advertising networks, and payment processors; the process, if any, by which an individual consumer may review and request changes to his or her personally identifiable information collected through the Web site or online service: Consumers may email privacy@acme.com to request access to or correction of their information; the process by which Acme, Inc. notifies consumers of material changes to this privacy policy: We will post an updated effective date and notify registered users by email; this privacy policy's effective date: October 1, 2026; and how Acme, Inc. responds to Web browser "do not track" signals or other mechanisms consumers may use to exercise choice regarding the collection of personally identifiable information about their online activities over time and across third-party Web sites or online services: We do not currently respond to Do Not Track browser signals.

CERTIFICATION
The undersigned, Jordan T. Reyes, certifies on behalf of Acme, Inc. that the privacy policy described in this information sheet has been conspicuously posted on Acme, Inc.'s Web site or online service at https://www.acme.com as of the date below, and that the disclosures above accurately describe that policy's content as of that date.

Signed: ______________________________
Jordan T. Reyes, on behalf of Acme, Inc.

citations.quote: (a) The term “personally identifiable information” means individually identifiable information about an individual consumer collected online by the operator from that individual and maintained by the operator in an accessible form, including any of the following: (1) A first and last name. (2) A home or other physical address, including street name and name of a city or town. (3) An e-mail address. (4) A telephone number. (5) A social security number. (6) Any other identifier that permits the physical or online contacting of a specific individual. (7) Information concerning a user that the Web site or online service collects online from the user and maintains in personally identifiable form in combination with an identifier described in this subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22577(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, definition of "operator"
citations.quote: (c) The term “operator” means any person or entity that owns a Web site located on the Internet or an online service that collects and maintains personally identifiable information from a consumer residing in California who uses or visits the Web site or online service if the Web site or online service is operated for commercial purposes. It does not include any third party that operates, hosts, or manages, but does not own, a Web site or online service on the owner’s behalf or by processing information on behalf of the owner.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes two subdivisions of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22577 — subdivision (a) (the definition of "personally identifiable information") and subdivision (c) (the definition of "operator") — because both are definitions the chapter applies throughout, and are grouped here rather than attached separately to each clause that uses the defined terms. This document's overall verified coverage of CalOPPA rests on two sections of the same chapter, § 22575 and § 22577, rather than on fully independent statutes; that is expected for a definitions section that exists to support the operative section, and is disclosed here for transparency. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause does not quote or verify subdivision (d)'s definition of "consumer," which was not independently checked for this clause; nor does it determine, for a specific business, whether a specific third-party vendor that hosts or manages a Web site on that business's behalf falls within the "operator" definition's exclusion or is itself an owner-operator — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

expectedJSON.body: California law defines "conspicuously post," with respect to a privacy policy, to include posting it by any of several methods: a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if that page is the homepage or the first significant page after entering the Web site; an icon that hyperlinks to a Web page where the actual policy is posted, if the icon is on the homepage or first significant page, contains the word "privacy," and uses a color that contrasts with the page's background or is otherwise distinguishable; a text link that hyperlinks to a Web page where the actual policy is posted, if the link is on the homepage or first significant page and either includes the word "privacy," is written in capital letters at least as large as the surrounding text, or is written in larger, contrasting, or otherwise set-off type that calls attention to it; any other functional hyperlink displayed so that a reasonable person would notice it; or, in the case of an online service, any other reasonably accessible means of making the privacy policy available to the online service's consumers.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22577(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, definition of "conspicuously post"
citations.quote: (b) The term “conspicuously post” with respect to a privacy policy shall include posting the privacy policy through any of the following: (1) A Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted if the Web page is the homepage or first significant page after entering the Web site. (2) An icon that hyperlinks to a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if the icon is located on the homepage or the first significant page after entering the Web site, and if the icon contains the word “privacy.” The icon shall also use a color that contrasts with the background color of the Web page or is otherwise distinguishable. (3) A text link that hyperlinks to a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if the text link is located on the homepage or first significant page after entering the Web site, and if the text link does one of the following: (A) Includes the word “privacy.” (B) Is written in capital letters equal to or greater in size than the surrounding text. (C) Is written in larger type than the surrounding text, or in contrasting type, font, or color to the surrounding text of the same size, or set off from the surrounding text of the same size by symbols or other marks that call attention to the language. (4) Any other functional hyperlink that is so displayed that a reasonable person would notice it. (5) In the case of an online service, any other reasonably accessible means of making the privacy policy available for consumers of the online service.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Business and Professions Code § 22577(b), in full, including its numbered paragraphs (1) through (5) and lettered subparagraphs (A) through (C). Paragraph (5) of this subdivision is the same alternative-means provision that § 22575(a), quoted in an earlier clause of this document, cross-references for an operator of an online service (as opposed to a Web site); the two clauses are therefore linked, though each independently quotes only its own subdivision. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause states the statutory test for what posting methods qualify as "conspicuous"; it does not determine whether a specific operator's actual Web page, icon, or link design in fact satisfies that test — that is a fact-specific, visual-design determination this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

expectedJSON.body: California law provides that an operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information from individual California-resident consumers who use or visit it is in violation of this chapter if it fails to comply with the posting requirement described elsewhere in this Notice, or with the provisions of its own posted privacy policy, and does so either knowingly and willfully, or negligently and materially — a mental-state and materiality threshold, rather than strict liability for any noncompliance. This chapter became operative on July 1, 2004. Separately, the Legislature declared that this chapter addresses a matter of statewide concern, and that it supersedes and preempts all rules, regulations, codes, ordinances, and other laws adopted by a city, county, city and county, municipality, or local agency regarding the posting of a privacy policy on an Internet Web site.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22576 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, violation standard: knowing and willful, or negligent and material, noncompliance
citations.quote: An operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information through the Web site or online service from individual consumers who use or visit the commercial Web site or online service and who reside in California shall be in violation of this section if the operator fails to comply with the provisions of Section 22575 or with the provisions of its posted privacy policy in either of the following ways: (a) Knowingly and willfully. (b) Negligently and materially.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22578 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, statewide concern and preemption of local privacy-posting laws
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that this chapter is a matter of statewide concern. This chapter supersedes and preempts all rules, regulations, codes, ordinances, and other laws adopted by a city, county, city and county, municipality, or local agency regarding the posting of a privacy policy on an Internet Web site.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22579 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, chapter operative date
citations.quote: This chapter shall become operative on July 1, 2004.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause draws on three separate statutory sections of the same chapter — Business and Professions Code §§ 22576 (the violation standard), 22578 (the preemption declaration), and 22579 (the chapter's operative date) — each independently verified and quoted from its own section rather than from subdivisions of one section, so each citation here is a genuinely separate authority within the chapter. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause does not address whether CalOPPA itself creates a private right of action for a consumer, or whether a violation might instead (or additionally) be pursued under some other statute, such as the Unfair Competition Law; that question was not researched for this clause and this document takes no position on it. The July 1, 2004 operative date and the chapter's 2003 enactment history are stated here for completeness of the compliance timeline; they are historical facts about when the chapter took effect, not a live deadline for an operator setting up a privacy policy today. No case law was checked on any of these three provisions; each statute's own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

expectedJSON.body: Acme, Inc. operates the commercial Web site or online service located at https://www.acme.com, which collects personally identifiable information through the Internet about individual consumers residing in California who use or visit it. Acme, Inc. conspicuously posts a privacy policy on that Web site or online service disclosing the following: the categories of personally identifiable information Acme, Inc. collects, and the categories of third-party persons or entities with whom Acme, Inc. may share that information: Identifiers (name, email address), internet activity (browsing history on our site), and geolocation data; the categories of third parties described further as: Analytics providers, advertising networks, and payment processors; the process, if any, by which an individual consumer may review and request changes to his or her personally identifiable information collected through the Web site or online service: Consumers may email privacy@acme.com to request access to or correction of their information; the process by which Acme, Inc. notifies consumers of material changes to this privacy policy: We will post an updated effective date and notify registered users by email; this privacy policy's effective date: October 1, 2026; and how Acme, Inc. responds to Web browser "do not track" signals or other mechanisms consumers may use to exercise choice regarding the collection of personally identifiable information about their online activities over time and across third-party Web sites or online services: We do not currently respond to Do Not Track browser signals.

The undersigned, Jordan T. Reyes, certifies on behalf of Acme, Inc. that the privacy policy described in this information sheet has been conspicuously posted on Acme, Inc.'s Web site or online service at https://www.acme.com as of the date below, and that the disclosures above accurately describe that policy's content as of that date.

Signed: ______________________________
Jordan T. Reyes, on behalf of Acme, Inc.
Date: September 1, 2026
